name: tool-search
title: Tool search: a smaller bag, still a bag
kicker: The machine web · what agents got next
html:
Tool search: a smaller bag, still a bag

What it gives, and it’s real

Tool definitions marked defer_loading: true stay out of the model’s context until a search over their names and descriptions (regex or BM25) finds them.

49 → 74%Opus 4 on MCP evaluations with large tool libraries (Anthropic’s figures)
79.5 → 88.1%Opus 4.5, same evaluations

Claude Code uses it too. It solves context size; HEART’s L1 and L2 solve the same with caching.

What it finds is still RPC

# a tool definition, illustrative
name: merge_pull_request
description: Merge a pull request.
input_schema:
  owner, repo, pull_number,
  merge_method: [merge, squash, rebase],
  sha
defer_loading: true

A function and its parameters: the same for every pull request, in every state. Chosen by the words of the task, not the state of anything.

Finds: the right functions to call. Never says: which acts are open now, on which address, or why not. That still arrives as an error after the call.

In fairness: MCP lets a server change its tool list during a session (notifications/tools/list_changed). That list belongs to the session, not to one resource’s representation.
say: To be fair to the newest answer. Tool search, which Anthropic ships on its API and which Claude Code itself uses, keeps tool definitions out of the model's context until a search over their names and descriptions finds them. That's a real gain: Anthropic reports, on MCP evaluations with large tool libraries, Opus 4 going from 49 to 74 percent, and Opus 4.5 from 79.5 to 88.1 percent, with it on. But look at what it finds. A definition is a function name, a description, and a JSON Schema for its arguments. The same for every pull request, in every state. It's chosen by relevance to the words of the task, not by the state of anything. Whether merging is allowed right now, on which address, and why not, still arrives only as an error after the call. Tool search makes the bag smaller. It's still the bag. And it's complementary: it solves context size, which HEART's L1 and L2 solve with caching; HEART solves what's valid now, and where. In fairness, MCP does let a server change its tool list during a session; but that list belongs to the session, not to one resource's representation.

deck:ref.name: in-band
deck:ref.label: IN-BAND
deck:ref.title: Instructions in every representation
deck:ref.summary: The media type is learned once; each representation carries the transitions available at that point.
deck:ref.quote:
“The media type identifies a specification that defines how a representation is to be processed. That is out-of-band information (all communication is dependent on some prior knowledge). What you are missing is that each representation contains the specific instructions for interfacing with a given service, provided in-band. The media type is a generic processing model that every agent can learn if there aren’t too many of them (hence the need for standards). The representation is specific to the application being performed by the agent. Each representation therefore provides the transitions that are available at that point in the application.

When representations are provided in hypertext form with typed relations (using microformats of HTML, RDF in N3 or XML, or even SVG), then automated agents can traverse these applications almost as well as any human. There are plenty of examples in the linked data communities. More important to me is that the same design reflects good human-Web design, and thus we can design the protocols to support both machine and human-driven applications by following the same architectural style.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, comment on “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: rule-6
deck:ref.label: R6 · BOOKMARK
deck:ref.title: Enter with a bookmark; follow what's offered
deck:ref.summary: In brief: one URI and known media types to start; every next step chosen from what the server put in the answer.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should be entered with no prior knowledge beyond the initial URI (bookmark) and set of standardized media types that are appropriate for the intended audience (i.e., expected to be understood by any client that might use the API). From that point on, all application state transitions must be driven by client selection of server-provided choices that are present in the received representations or implied by the user’s manipulation of those representations. The transitions may be determined (or limited by) the client’s knowledge of media types and resource communication mechanisms, both of which may be improved on-the-fly (e.g., code-on-demand). [Failure here implies that out-of-band information is driving interaction instead of hypertext.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”
